report.summary: The release overhauls how this logging library writes, formats, and colors its console output, so terminal logs may look different and need a visual check.
keyChanges: Log line assembly for both console reporters moved into a shared preparation step built on new helpers for argument formatting, format-template compilation, date formatting, and cached color resolution, keeping the visible layout of timestamp, uppercased type, tag, message, extra arguments, colors, and icons unchanged.

The write step now takes a settings object with an error flag and a write mode instead of a raw output stream, routes error-level entries to the error output itself, and supports synchronous and asynchronous writing, while the logging call's second argument changed from a boolean asynchronous flag to a mode string so a leftover boolean now falls back to the default write path instead of the earlier promise behavior.

The styled reporter's console-clear step still invokes the write step without the settings object the new signature expects, and color resolution now accepts named colors and hex values through a cache feeding each styled line's text, background, and additional colors, icon, and icon spacing.

Seven separate sync, async, and error output routines in the console reporter were consolidated into one routine that picks the normal or error stream from an error flag, so error entries logged synchronously — which previously were written to the normal output stream — should now go to the error stream.

The default log-line template changed from numbered placeholders like %1$s to named ones like %date$s and is now filled by new shared format helpers instead of the previous printf-style and date libraries; the old template's fourth placeholder was malformed (missing its % sign), so field placement could previously render incorrectly.
Tag rendering was reworked: the old step that rewrote colons in tags and appended separators is gone, so tags, especially those containing ':', may render differently.

Default options (normal stream, error stream, HH:mm:ss time format, format templates) moved to a shared constant while caller options still override them, and the reporter no longer pre-binds its write methods when constructed.
The main logger module now imports a helper from a relocated utilities folder with no intended behavior change, but every application using the library must still start and log normally.

Log lines are now written through a new stream writer offering default, async, and sync modes; both the basic reporter's log output and the fancy reporter's clear-and-redraw path route through it, so console output should appear complete and in order on the correct stream.

The standard log line layouts are now precompiled and cached, so rendered entries should be laid out exactly as the templates define: bracketed timestamp, padded type, tag, message, additional detail lines, and color segments.

Background colors are resolved by name or hex code and cached, but a repeated color name returns the internal cache table itself instead of the cached color, so the second use of the same background color may render incorrectly; this is the top regression suspect in this group.

Log line templates were rewritten from numbered to named placeholders and the separate line-preparation step was merged into the main log flow; the layout (icon, tag, colored message, extra arguments) should stay the same, but any mismatch will show as garbled, mis-colored, or literal-placeholder terminal output.
Plain log entries previously printed no icon at all; the new logic falls back to the default arrow icon, so simple log lines may now start with an arrow where they previously showed nothing.

Badge-style highlighted lines previously used a dedicated background-color helper (colored background with black text, including hex colors); that helper was removed and the badge color slot now reuses the ordinary text-color helper, so badges may render as colored text instead of an inverse highlighted block.

Default icons and format templates moved into one overridable defaults object, so custom reporter options can now replace icons and formats wholesale; with no custom options, the default per-level symbols must still appear.
qaChecks: Verify that a log entry requesting a console clear still clears the terminal and then prints its message without throwing an error or losing the line.

Verify styled lines show the expected icon, text and background colors, a highlighted badge type when requested, and any extra arguments on their own lines, with no unrendered placeholder tokens left in the output.
Verify log entries with a custom color, including a hex color value, still render with the intended text and background colors.
Verify error-level entries are written to the error output stream while normal entries go to standard output.
Verify logging that runs in asynchronous mode still writes every line and completes rather than being cut off or reordered.
Confirm that a log call still writes its message when given the old boolean-style asynchronous flag instead of a mode string, since such calls now take the default write path.

Verify each line still shows the timestamp in the configured time format, the uppercased log type, the tag when present and empty when absent, the message, and extra arguments or a formatted stack trace on the following lines.

Verify an info line renders with the time in brackets, the entry type right-padded inside brackets, then the tag, the message, and any extra data (an object argument as formatted JSON) each appearing exactly once and in order, and that no raw template tokens such as %date$s or 4$s leak into the output.

Test an error entry in synchronous mode with redirected output: the error text must appear only in the error-output file while info lines stay in the normal-output file — previously synchronous error output was written to the normal output stream.

Check a tag containing a colon (for example my:tag) renders as readable text with no '>' characters or trailing separators, and an entry with no tag leaves no stray separator or doubled space between the type and the message.

Verify the burst completes without dropped or duplicated lines and the asynchronous log promise settles once the output drains, and confirm asynchronous and synchronous runs produce the same set of lines.
Ensure custom streams, time format, and format templates still override the built-in defaults.

Validate a custom format template written in the old numbered-placeholder style (for example %1$s) still produces a complete, readable line rather than mangled text, since the placeholder style changed from numbered to named.
Confirm an application using the library with no configuration starts and logs normally.

Verify the second of two consecutive same-type log entries still shows its background-colored type badge correctly, with no garbled text, dumped object content, or crash; the repeated color is the input that triggers the cache path.
Verify a hex color such as #ff0000 and a named color each render their intended background color on the log entry.
Verify a rapid burst of many log messages, or one very long message, appears complete and in order with nothing dropped or duplicated; this exercises the wait-until-stream-drains path.
Verify error-level messages go to the error output while normal messages go to standard output.
Verify a log message emitted while the fancy reporter is displaying in-progress output clears and redraws the screen cleanly, without leftover or interleaved text.

Verify a standard log entry shows the bracketed timestamp in the expected time format, the type padded to a fixed width, the tag, the message, and any additional detail lines with correct spacing and colors.

Check: log one message that has a tag and two extra arguments, and confirm the line shows the tag, the colored message, and the extras on their own following line, with no literal placeholder text (for example %message$s) and no color codes bleeding into the next line.

Verify: log a plain message with no explicit type and no custom icon, and confirm what appears at the start of the line; the previous version printed no icon for plain log entries while the new code shows the default arrow icon, so flag it if plain logs are expected to stay icon-free.

Confirm: the type label on a badge line still renders as a clearly set-off, readable highlighted block; it previously used a true background color with black text and the new code applies the ordinary text color in that slot, so flag any change from background block to plain colored text.
Validate: with a hex color on a badge line, confirm the highlighting still appears; hex colors previously produced a matching background and that dedicated handling was removed.

Ensure: each level still shows its expected symbol (dot, i, check, cross, warning, ellipsis, heart, arrow) in the expected color when no custom options are passed, since icons now come from the new defaults object.

Test: pass an icons object that defines only one level and confirm the other levels still render sensibly; options replace the whole matching defaults section, so unlisted levels fall back to the default arrow icon rather than keeping their per-level symbols.
uncertainty: The console-clear step invokes the write step without the settings object the new signature requires, so a log entry that asks to clear the console appears likely to fail at runtime; confirm the final combined behavior once all changes in this release are merged.

The new shared formatting and stream-writing helpers were not included in the evidence, so the exact new rendering of tags, empty fields, and custom format templates — especially templates in the old numbered-placeholder style — could not be confirmed and should be compared line-by-line against previous output.

No direct caller of the background-color helper appears in the dependency evidence, so the exact reporter path that triggers the repeated-color defect is unconfirmed; if colored log badges do not route through it, the repeat-color check may not exercise the fault.

It is not documented whether badges are still meant to render with a true background color: the only background-color helper was removed and the badge slot now reuses the text-color helper, so the intended new badge appearance (background block versus colored text, especially for hex colors) needs product confirmation.

report.summary: This release changes how drawings are shown, saved, copied, and undone, so the overall impact is that artwork and editing should still look and behave the same.
keyChanges: On-screen editing now draws shapes, lines, arrows, and text from a per-element offscreen image that is cached between frames and rebuilt whenever the zoom level changes, which speeds up interactive rendering but does not guarantee pixel-perfect output, so an element whose appearance changes without triggering a rebuild could show stale artwork.

Exports to canvas, PNG, JPEG, and SVG deliberately bypass the new cache and draw every element directly, and they now position content using the scene's own scroll offsets instead of the separate offset overrides that were removed, so the on-screen view and the exported file may differ subtly, particularly for elements at fractional pixel positions.

Text elements now render through the same path as shapes while keeping the existing behavior of splitting multiline text onto separate lines and applying font, color, and opacity, and zoom handling for the whole scene was consolidated into a single save-apply-reset sequence shared by elements, the selection marquee, selection outlines, and resize handles.

Dragging a selection marquee now ends the render pass early, which means scrollbars are not painted while the marquee is active, and the visible-elements result returned at that point is what tells the editor whether the entire drawing has been scrolled outside the visible canvas.

Exported output (PNG, SVG, clipboard copies, and the export dialog preview) is now positioned using a floored whole-number scroll offset instead of a separate fractional offset, so drawings with elements at fractional coordinates can shift by up to 1 pixel and risk clipped edges or reduced padding in exports.

The editor canvas now re-renders with render optimizations enabled after updates, and resizing the window clears every element's cached rendering, so stale, missing, or leftover strokes after edits or window resizes are the main regression risk.

Automatic saving to browser storage no longer excludes selection-type elements before saving, so a selection captured at save time could persist and reappear as a stray artifact after reloading the page.

Opening saved scenes, shareable links, and browser-storage restores now floors scroll offsets to whole numbers and resets each element's cached rendering with canvas offsets defaulting to 0, so loaded drawings should render completely and stay centered as before.
Copying or cutting selected elements now strips each element's cached rendering from the in-app clipboard snapshot; previously that cached field was included in the serialized copy data.
Undo and redo snapshots likewise now record the cached rendering as empty instead of serializing it, so restored elements come back without a stale cached image.

Browser autosave (about 300 milliseconds after edits, and again when the page unloads) now stores elements without the cached-rendering field, so newly saved scenes differ in format from previously saved ones.

The canvas renderer's separate zoom-scaling and zoom-translation helper steps were consolidated into a single zoom-application step used by the editor canvas and the export preview; output is expected to be identical but the change does not prove it pixel-identical.
The remaining edits are type-only declarations that scroll positions are whole numbers and have no runtime effect on their own.

All ways of moving the canvas view, including mouse-wheel scrolling, drag panning, and dragging the on-canvas scrollbars, now round the scroll position down to whole canvas pixels instead of keeping fractional sub-pixel offsets.

This changes movement granularity when zoomed in: a scroll step smaller than one on-screen pixel that previously shifted the view fractionally now rounds down to a full pixel (a 0.5-pixel step at 2x zoom becomes 1 pixel), and crossing below the drawing's origin can jump an extra pixel because negative values also round down.

The coordinate conversion and scrollbar helpers now formally require whole-pixel scroll values; this is a type-level contract with no intended runtime change, and image export shares this rendering path, so exports should come out unchanged.

Every newly created element now starts with an initialized per-element render cache (empty canvas, cache zoom 1, zero offsets) and text elements are explicitly created without a cached shape; nothing should look different, but selection, hit-testing, and resize read this element data.
qaChecks: Verify all six element types still render with correct stroke, fill, and transparency while panning the canvas around, because panning exercises the new cached rendering path for every element.

Test zooming in and out repeatedly on the same elements and confirm every element redraws sharply at each zoom level, since the cached image must be rebuilt whenever the zoom level changes and a missed rebuild would show a blurry or wrongly scaled element.
Test an element dragged so it sits at a fractional on-screen position and confirm it does not shift, jitter, or double-draw between the cached and direct rendering paths.
Check that a multiline text element, including one with blank lines, still places each line at the same position and keeps its font, color, and opacity.

Verify the selection marquee dragged on empty canvas still covers exactly the area under the cursor while the view is panned and zoomed, since marquee positioning moved into the shared rendering path.

Confirm the dashed outline and resize handles around a selected element stay aligned with the element at several zoom levels, because zoom is now applied and reset as one unit around each of these layers.
Test resizing a single selected element and confirm the element and its outline update together with no offset artwork left behind.
Verify an exported image contains every element at the correct position and size with the usual margin preserved, since export positioning now always uses the scene's own scroll offsets.
Confirm an exported SVG still shows shapes, arrows, and multiline text correctly, because SVG export now shares the element preparation logic that also feeds the new cached rendering.
Test exporting with the background on and off and at a scale other than 1 and confirm the output stays complete and correctly positioned.

Test panning all content off the visible canvas and confirm the editor correctly recognizes that nothing is visible, then pan back and confirm it recovers, because that recognition now flows through the render pass that ends early during marquee dragging.

Verify exporting a drawing whose elements sit at fractional coordinates as PNG, SVG, and clipboard copy keeps every element fully inside the image with visible padding, with nothing clipped and no shift larger than about 1 pixel at any edge.
Confirm the preview image shown in the export dialog matches the downloaded export in position and completeness.
Verify drawing, moving, resizing, undoing, and redoing several elements leaves every stroke fully rendered, with no leftover fragments, blank shapes, or stale outlines.
Verify resizing the browser window larger and smaller keeps all elements rendered correctly and crisp afterwards.
Check that after selecting several elements, waiting past the autosave delay, and reloading the page, the drawing reappears complete with no stray selection rectangle or other leftover artifacts.
Verify a scene saved by the previous version reloads with all elements rendering in their original positions and offsets.
Verify opening a saved file or shareable link centers the whole drawing in view with nothing cut off, including a drawing whose center lands on fractional coordinates.
Test the round trip of saving a drawing to a shareable link and reopening it; the reopened scene should match the original in content and position.
Ensure mouse-wheel scrolling and scrollbar dragging keep elements aligned and crisp, with no growing drift after many small scroll steps.

Verify that after the shapes have been rendered on screen, selecting them and copying (Ctrl+C) then pasting (Ctrl+V) creates duplicates that look identical to the originals and can be selected, moved, resized, and edited.
Check that pasted copies show no rendering artifacts such as a blank, frozen, or misdrawn appearance compared with the originals.
Verify that cutting (Ctrl+X) removes the selected shapes and a following paste re-creates them with correct appearance and full editability.
Verify that drawing shapes, waiting at least one second for autosave, and reloading the page restores the complete drawing, rendered correctly and still editable.
Check that an edit made immediately before closing or reloading the tab is still present when the app is opened again.
Confirm that a drawing already in browser storage from an earlier build loads, renders correctly, and remains editable.
Verify several undo and redo cycles after drawing, moving, and resizing shapes: each redo restores the exact previous state and shapes render correctly after every undo and redo.
Check that after undo and redo, elements can still be selected and edited without rendering glitches appearing.

Verify that zooming in and out several levels and panning repeatedly keeps shapes, their selection outlines, and the scrollbars aligned, with no progressive drift, blur, or offset after multiple interactions.
Verify that the preview in the export dialog and a saved PNG or SVG export show all content with the usual border padding, matching the on-canvas view, with nothing clipped or shifted.

Verify slow trackpad wheel scrolling at 2x zoom still moves the viewport smoothly in the correct direction without stalling or jumping, using scroll steps small enough to shift less than one pixel, which previously moved the view fractionally and now round down to whole pixels.
Verify panning the canvas by dragging keeps elements aligned under the cursor during the drag and the view comes to rest on a whole-pixel position on release.
Verify dragging the horizontal and vertical scrollbars moves the scene as before and the thumb tracks the pointer correctly under the new whole-pixel rounding.
Ensure panning past the drawing's top-left origin (scroll going negative) and back does not jump an extra pixel or get stuck at the zero boundary.
Ensure an image export taken after panning the canvas shows exactly the same visible portion as the on-screen canvas, with no one-pixel shift from the new scroll rounding.
Ensure shapes and text in the exported image are positioned and rendered identically to the on-screen view.
Verify pasting a copied group of elements while the canvas is panned and zoomed places the group centered at the cursor position as before.
Verify pasting text creates a text element that renders correctly at the paste location and can be selected and edited.

Verify newly drawn shapes and text render correctly at different zoom levels and can be clicked, selected, and resized with the usual handles and cursor behavior, since new elements now carry initialized render-cache fields that these interactions read.
uncertainty: While a selection marquee is being dragged the render pass now finishes before scrollbars are painted, so it is unresolved whether scrollbars are meant to stay visible during a drag-select; QA should watch for scrollbars disappearing mid-drag and report the observed behavior.

The old autosave deliberately excluded selection-type elements and the new code saves everything, but the supplied evidence does not show whether such elements still occur in the saved list; if stray selection artifacts appear after reload this change is the likely cause, while a clean reload check may mean the change is harmless.

Drawings saved by the previous build may contain the cached-rendering field that new saves now omit, and whether the loading path fully ignores that old field is not established by this change set; if a pre-update drawing renders incorrectly after reload, flag it rather than assuming the new save format is at fault.

Rounding every scroll step to whole pixels slightly changes scroll feel at zoomed-in levels and the supplied evidence does not state this is intended; if any panning entry point elsewhere in this release still stores a fractional scroll position, the new whole-pixel scroll contract would be broken and the view could misalign.

report.summary: The drawing editor now lets you rotate elements, and selecting, resizing, text editing, copying, and exporting all respect that rotation.
keyChanges: Selecting an element now shows a new circular rotation handle above it; dragging it rotates the element around its center, and the dashed selection outline and square resize handles now rotate with the element instead of staying axis-aligned.

Pointer hit-testing now recognizes the rotation handle first, so clicking it starts a rotation drag rather than a move or resize; text elements now show only this handle and can be rotated while resizing stays disabled (previously text had no handles at all).

Element bounding boxes now account for rotation, so image exports and copy-as-image cover the full rotated shape (previously rotated corners could fall outside the export area), pasted rotated content centers on the cursor, and scroll-to-content and scrollbars reflect the rotated extent.
Element painting now rotates around each element's center on both the cached-image and the direct redraw paths, so rotated shapes, lines, and arrows display at the correct angle and position.

Selected elements gain a rotation handle that sets their angle around the center; holding Shift snaps the angle to 22.5-degree steps, the handle shows an east-west resize cursor, and the temporary rotating state is cleared when the pointer is released and is excluded from the state saved to local storage.

Resizing now accounts for the element's angle: pointer movement is counter-rotated and a new rotation-aware positioning routine keeps the opposite corner or edge anchored; for unrotated elements the result matches the previous behavior exactly.
The on-canvas text editor now tilts with the element's angle, and a brand-new text element is created at angle 0 so its editing box stays untilted.

Restoring drawings from files, share links or the backend, local storage, and live-collaboration updates now defaults a missing angle to 0, so older scenes load upright instead of carrying an undefined angle.

Every drawn element now stores a rotation angle, and click-selection reverse-rotates the clicked position around the element's center before testing, so rotated elements are selected by their visible rotated outline instead of their unrotated bounding box; unrotated elements (everything newly created, which defaults to angle 0) select exactly as before.
The selection overlay gains a rotation handle placed about 16 pixels above the shape, and the corner resize handles are rotated to sit on a rotated element's actual corners.
Text editing started by double-click or Enter now passes the element's angle to the on-canvas text editor, so the editing box appears rotated to match rotated text instead of always being horizontal.

Editing hints changed: the resize hint now shows only when the last pointer-down was with a mouse, and a new rotate hint shows while rotating with a mouse; with pen or touch input the resize hint that previously appeared no longer shows.

SVG export now applies each element's rotation: the per-element transform changed from a plain translation to a translation plus a rotation around the element's own center, so rotated rectangles, ellipses, diamonds, lines and arrows, and text export at the angle shown on the canvas instead of flat as before.
The same rendering feeds the export dialog, whole-drawing and selected-area image export, and the copy-to-clipboard-as-PNG action, so all of these outputs should now show rotation consistently.
Unrotated elements only gain an identity rotation in their transform, so drawings with no rotated elements should export exactly as before.
A new editor-state flag that tracks whether an element is being rotated was added along with type-only edits and blank lines, none of which change runtime behavior in this group.
qaChecks: Verify that selecting a shape shows a circular rotation handle above it and dragging that handle rotates the shape around its center while the dashed outline and square handles stay attached to the rotated shape.
Verify that with a rectangle rotated to 45 degrees, dragging each drawn square handle resizes the rotated shape and grabbing the circular handle starts a rotation drag rather than moving or resizing.
Verify that selecting a text element shows only the circular rotation handle and dragging it rotates the text while its size stays unchanged.
Confirm that no square resize handles appear for a selected text element and dragging from its corners does not resize it.
Verify that exporting the rotated rectangle as PNG and as SVG produces an image containing the entire rotated shape with an even margin and no clipped corners.
Verify that copying the rotated rectangle to the clipboard as an image captures the full rotated shape, not just its unrotated box.
Verify that pasting the copied rotated element places it centered under the pointer with its rotation intact.
Verify that rotated shapes, lines, and arrows render at the correct angle and position at normal zoom, when zoomed in and out, and on a high-DPI display.
Verify that reopening the saved drawing centers the view on the rotated content and that the scrollbars match its true extent.

Verify dragging the rotation handle of a selected rectangle spins it around its center to any angle, the cursor over that handle is an east-west resize cursor, and releasing the pointer ends the rotation so the very next drag resizes instead of rotating.
Verify holding Shift while dragging the rotation handle snaps the angle in 22.5-degree steps through a full turn, including where the angle wraps past a full circle.

Verify rotating a rectangle to about 45 degrees and then dragging each of its four corner handles and four edge handles, one pass with Shift held to lock width and height together: the opposite corner or edge must stay anchored and the shape must grow along its tilted axes, because the previous code positioned tilted elements as if upright and shifted them wrongly during resize.
Verify an unrotated rectangle and a two-point arrow still resize from every handle exactly as before this release, with the anchored corner or endpoint staying put.

Verify double-clicking a text element rotated to a clear angle (for example 45 degrees) opens the editing box tilted to match the element and positioned over it, and that committing the text by clicking away or pressing Escape keeps the text at that rotated angle and position.
Verify adding a brand-new text element on the canvas opens an untilted editing box at the click point and saves the text normally, since new text starts at angle 0.
Verify rotating elements, then reloading the page: the drawing is restored with the same tilts and the canvas is not left stuck in a resizing or rotating state.

Verify opening an older drawing file saved before this release that stores no angle (for example by dropping it onto the canvas): every element loads upright and can then be selected, resized, and rotated normally.
Verify a drawing containing rotated elements survives a save-and-reopen round trip through a file or shareable link with identical tilts.
Ensure an element rotated by one participant appears with the same tilt for the other participants, including when the receiving side already shows an older, unrotated copy of that element.

Verify that after rotating the thin rectangle about 45 degrees, clicking its visually rotated middle, ends, and edges selects it, while clicking an empty corner of its old upright bounding box does not.

Confirm unrotated elements still select as before: click the center of the filled rectangle to select it, and click the transparent rectangle only within a thin border margin (about 10 pixels at default zoom), not in its empty interior.
Test a drawing saved with the previous version: open it and click its shapes, lines, and text to confirm each still selects where it visually is.
Verify that selecting an element shows a rotation handle about 16 pixels above the selection box in addition to the usual corner handles.
Confirm that after rotating an element, its corner resize handles sit on the rotated corners rather than on an upright bounding box.
Check that all newly created shapes, lines/arrows, and text appear unrotated and can immediately be selected and dragged.
Verify that double-clicking rotated text opens the editing box rotated to match the text's angle and that after confirming, the text stays rotated and in place.
Confirm double-clicking unrotated text still opens a horizontal editor at its center and saving keeps the text unchanged.
Ensure pressing Enter with a single selected element still opens the text editor at the element's center without errors.
Verify with a mouse that dragging a corner to resize shows the resize hint and rotating the element shows the new rotate hint.
Confirm with touch or pen input that resizing shows no resize or rotate hint anymore (previously the resize hint appeared for every pointer type).
Validate in a non-English language that rotating with the mouse still shows the rotate hint (translated or English fallback) with no blank hint or error.
Verify each element rotated to 45 degrees on the canvas appears in the exported SVG at that same angle and position; rotated elements previously exported flat.
Verify the unrotated comparison elements export unchanged, with no shift, size change, or extra tilt.
Verify the rotated two-line text keeps its line breaks and angle, and that a simple straight arrow exports without errors and at the correct angle.
Check that after rotating an element to 45 degrees, copying the canvas as PNG and pasting it into another application shows the element rotated exactly as on the canvas, not flat.
Ensure copy-as-PNG still works for an unrotated drawing from both the canvas context menu and the keyboard shortcut.
Test exporting the full drawing and confirm every element keeps its own rotation and relative position.
Test exporting only a selection of rotated elements and confirm the selected subset exports with correct rotation and spacing relative to each other.
uncertainty: No navigation details, menus, routes, or page surfaces were supplied for this release, so the route to the editor canvas could not be confirmed and testers should use the editor entry point they normally use.

The evidence confirms the click-to-create text path passes angle 0 explicitly, but it does not confirm that every path into editing or creating text always supplies a valid angle to the editing overlay; if a path omits it, the overlay could lose its centering and scaling and appear misplaced over the element, which the new-text and rotated-text double-click checks are designed to surface.

Element data now requires an angle, but no load-time default is evidenced for drawings saved before this update or received from older clients; if such elements reach the canvas without an angle, click-selection could misbehave. The old-drawing check in the first test area covers the visible symptom; report any element that stops responding to clicks.

A new flag tracking whether an element is being rotated was added to the editor state, but nothing in this group sets or reads it, so any user-visible rotation-mode interaction that depends on it ships in other groups of this release and cannot be verified here.

report.summary: This release adds element grouping to the drawing editor, letting users group and ungroup shapes that are then treated as single units when selecting, editing, copying, and saving or exporting.
keyChanges: Selecting any element that belongs to a group - by dragging a selection box or by clicking - now selects the entire group automatically, and the canvas draws a single selection outline around each selected group; previously only the individually picked elements were selected.

Clearing selection changed: clicking empty canvas now clears element selection, group selection, and any active group-editing mode together (previously only element selection was cleared, leaving stale group state), and a plain click on an element no longer wipes the selection while a group is selected.

Duplicating by dragging now gives the duplicates their own group memberships consistent with the group being edited, instead of copying the originals' group IDs, so a duplicated group should be independent of the original.

The Group, Ungroup, and Select All actions now use the new group-selection logic: a group created while editing an existing group is inserted at the correct nesting level, ungrouping removes only the selected group levels, and Select All also marks groups as selected.

Group editing is now first-class on the canvas: the editor state tracks which group is being edited and which groups are selected, so clicking a member of a grouped set selects the whole group, while clicking outside the edited group, on empty canvas, switching to a shape tool, or releasing Space with a shape tool active exits group editing.

Double-clicking a member of a selected group now enters group editing with only that element selected — previously it opened the text editor — and inserting a text element now also clears any group editing state.
Pasting elements while a group is being edited now adds the pasted copies to that group, keeping duplicated sets grouped.

Restored and imported drawings now guarantee every element has a group list (empty by default), so older files without group data load safely, groups survive save/load, and saved or share-link payloads now include the two new group state fields.
Group and ungroup actions are now wired into the editor, and every newly created element (shape, line, text) starts with an empty group list.
Select All (Ctrl/Cmd+A) now selects whole groups and exits any group-editing context; before, it only marked every non-deleted element as individually selected and left the editing state untouched.

Duplicating now preserves group structure with fresh group ids: duplicates of a grouped element form their own new group instead of sharing the source's group membership, and while a group is being edited the duplicate stays inside that edited group (outer groups get fresh ids); one shared id map per operation keeps copies of the same group together across the duplicate action, alt-drag duplication, and paste.
No visual change is intended from the new empty group field itself, but it reaches rendering, selection, and export (including the export watermark), so those are smoke-test surfaces.

The editor gains element grouping: selecting two or more elements and pressing Ctrl+G (Cmd+G on Mac, without Shift) combines them into one unit that moves and selects together, and Shift+Ctrl+G ungroups; Group and Ungroup entries are also added to the canvas context menu.

These actions deliberately do nothing and record no undo-history entry when grouping fewer than two elements, when the selection is exactly one complete group, or when ungrouping with no group selected; a real group or ungroup is recorded so undo restores it.

Selection outlines changed on the canvas: elements selected as part of a group no longer get an individual dashed outline each; one dashed outline is drawn around the whole group's outer bounds, and an outline also appears around the group currently being edited.
Exports and clipboard copies run through the same rendering routine, so drawings containing groups should be checked in PNG/SVG output.

The keyboard shortcuts dialog now documents two new shortcuts: Group (Ctrl+G, shown as Cmd+G on Mac) and Ungroup (Ctrl+Shift+G, shown as Cmd+Shift+G on Mac), so the on-screen reference must match actual grouping behavior.
The two new labels come from the translation system, so if any language is missing one of these labels the shortcuts dialog fails to open, making translations the main regression risk of this change.

Drawing elements now carry the list of groups they belong to as part of their stored data; this underpins grouping but has no standalone runtime effect, so it needs no separate test beyond the grouping checks.
qaChecks: Verify that dragging a selection box that encloses only one member of a grouped pair selects the entire group: both members show as selected and one selection outline spans the whole group rather than just the boxed member.
Confirm that clicking (without dragging) a member of the currently selected group keeps the group selected instead of clearing the selection.

Test duplicating by dragging while holding the duplicate modifier (typically Alt) on a member of a grouped pair: the duplicates should arrive as their own group so moving one duplicate moves both duplicates together, and moving the duplicates must not move the originals or vice versa.
Confirm that double-clicking a member of a selected group enters the group so subsequent clicks select individual members inside it rather than re-selecting the whole group.

Ensure that a click on empty canvas while a group is selected clears element selection and group selection together, so the next click starts a fresh single-element selection with no lingering group behavior.
Test that after entering group editing, a single click on empty canvas exits group editing as well as clearing the selection.
Verify that grouping two or more selected elements makes them act as one unit and leaves the new group selected with all members highlighted.

Test nested grouping: while editing a group (after double-clicking in), select a subset and group again; the new sub-group should sit inside the outer group, and Ungroup at the outer level should remove only that level while the inner group still moves as one.
Confirm that Ungroup on a selected group separates its members into individually selectable elements that remain selected.
Validate Select All with mixed grouped and ungrouped elements: every element is selected and groups are treated as selected, so a following Ungroup removes all group memberships at once.
Ensure exporting or copying the drawing as an image while a group is selected still renders every grouped element in the output with no stray selection decorations.
Check that clicking one member of a grouped set selects all members of that group together as one selection (previously only the clicked element was selected).

Test with two grouped shapes selected as a group: double-click one member — the app should switch to editing just that element inside the group (only it stays selected) instead of opening the text editor as before.
Ensure that clicking an element outside the group being edited, or clicking empty canvas, exits group editing and clears both element and group selection.
Confirm that switching to a shape tool, or pressing and releasing the Space key while a shape tool is active, exits group editing, and that clearing the canvas leaves no stale group selection.
Verify that double-clicking on empty canvas, or on an element that is not part of the selected group, still starts text editing as before.
Check that creating a text element while a group is being edited exits group editing once the text is inserted.

Confirm that a text element inside a group is still editable: enter group editing on it with a double-click, then open the text editor for that single element (for example with the Enter key) and save the text.
Test copying grouped elements and pasting: the pasted copies appear at the cursor, are selected after pasting, and remain grouped with each other.
Check that pasting while editing a group adds the pasted elements to that group, so they move and select together with the group afterwards.
Verify that a drawing containing groups saves and reopens with groups intact: members still select together and nothing errors.
Check that opening an older drawing whose elements have no group data loads without errors and elements behave normally.

Confirm that creating a shareable link or saving to the backend while grouped elements exist succeeds, and opening the shared drawing shows the groups (the shared payload now also carries the new group state fields).

Test selecting a single member of a group and exporting or copying the image: the output should include every member of the group, since selecting one member now selects the whole group (previously only the clicked element).
Ensure a scene containing groups exports fully with all grouped elements rendered in the image.
Confirm selecting several elements and grouping them works, and ungrouping splits them again (these actions are newly wired into the editor).

Verify duplicating a selected group creates an independent copy: the copies form their own group, dragging one copy moves only the copies, and the original group is untouched (previously a duplicate would have shared the source's group membership).
Verify duplicating the whole group in one operation keeps all copies in a single new group, and alt-dragging a grouped element to duplicate it also yields a separate new group.

Test duplicating while a group is being edited — the duplicate should stay inside the edited group rather than become a separate group — and duplicating an element from a drawing saved before this change, which should not error.
Check that Ctrl/Cmd+A selects every non-deleted element — shapes, lines, and text — and still excludes deleted elements.
Check that while editing a group, Ctrl/Cmd+A exits the group-editing context: afterwards, clicking one member of that group selects the whole group (previously the editing state was left untouched).
Verify pasting a copied group produces one new independent group: moving a pasted element moves only the pasted group and the source group is unaffected.
Verify pasting the same group twice creates two separate groups, one per paste.
Confirm a fresh rectangle, a line or arrow, and a text element are each created, selectable, and movable as before (new elements now carry an empty group list).
Ensure exporting as PNG or SVG with the watermark option enabled, and copying to clipboard as PNG or SVG, produce output that looks unchanged.

Verify: select two or more separate shapes and press Ctrl+G (Cmd+G on Mac, without Shift) — they become one group: dragging any member moves all of them, a single dashed outline wraps the whole group instead of one outline per shape, and Ctrl+Z restores the original ungrouped shapes.

Check: select exactly one complete existing group and press Ctrl+G — nothing changes and no duplicate or nested group is created.

Test: select a group and press Shift+Ctrl+G (Shift+Cmd+G on Mac) — the group is dissolved so members move and select independently again; also confirm Shift+Ctrl+G with no group selected does nothing and does not accidentally group.

uncertainty: The supplied context does not establish what a plain click on an element outside the currently selected groups should do now that the old clear-on-click rule is skipped whenever a group is selected (the old behavior cleared the whole selection); record the actual behavior during group-selection testing and flag it if the selection appears stuck.

With a group selected, double-click no longer opens the text editor for a member element, and the supplied context documents no visible alternative path for editing grouped text, so whether grouped text stays easily editable is the key open question.

The new duplication logic reads each element's group list directly, and elements saved before this change may not have one; duplicating elements from older drawings is the most likely regression and is covered by the check in the first test area.

The renderer now also draws a dashed outline around the group currently being edited, but the supplied context does not describe how a user enters group editing mode, so that outline has no navigation path or check; verify it manually if group editing is reachable in this build.

The translation keys for the new labels were not changed in this group, so whether every supported language provides them is unconfirmed; verify the dialog opens in each available language, especially non-English ones.

report.summary: This release reworks how lines and arrows are edited on the drawing canvas, letting testers select, move, add, and delete individual points, with related changes to keyboard shortcuts, on-canvas hints, and undo behavior.
keyChanges: In point-edit mode (select a line or arrow and press Enter), pressing on a point handle and moving the pointer now drags that point and reshapes the element; while a point is dragged, other pointer-move behavior such as panning or element dragging is skipped.

On pointer release in point-edit mode, a dragged start or end point within the snapping threshold of the opposite endpoint closes the loop; a closed loop fills with its background color and can then be dragged from its interior.

Holding Alt in point-edit mode appends a trailing point that follows the cursor and commits on click, while releasing Alt and moving away removes the uncommitted point; clicking near a point selects it, with the hit radius scaled by zoom plus one pixel for the outline.

Deleting the active point reuses the same point-move logic; deleting the first point re-anchors the remaining points so the drawn shape stays put, and deleting down to a single point removes the whole element.

Element updates now skip a point update whose coordinates are all unchanged (no version bump, re-render, or collaborator sync), and the scene rebuilds a by-id element map whenever all elements are replaced, so point editing must still find elements after undo, paste, or a collaborator update.

Selecting exactly one line, arrow, or freehand stroke and pressing Enter or double-clicking (double-tapping on touch) now enters a point-editing mode that shows a circle handle on every point; previously Enter did nothing on these elements and double-click opened a text box.

While point-editing, canvas clicks and pointer moves are rerouted to the point editor: points can be grabbed, dragged, and added, the element's resize handles and selection outline are hidden (also while drawing a multi-point line), and the point under the pointer is highlighted.
If the element being edited is deleted or otherwise deselected, the app automatically finalizes and exits point-editing mode.
The point-editing state is stripped from the local-browser autosave and defaults to empty, so reloading or restoring never resumes a half-finished edit.
Exports and clipboard images render through the same scene renderer as the editor, so exporting during point editing can leak the red editing handles into the output and needs one visual check.

Point editing for lines and arrows now runs through a dedicated editor module; entering edit mode re-normalizes the shape's points (first point pinned to the element origin with the element position shifted to compensate), so the drawing must look unchanged and stay in place when entering and leaving edit mode.
Dragging a point is now sticky and rotation-aware: once a drag starts, the same point keeps following the cursor even when the pointer moves off the handle or the element is rotated.

Point adding changed: holding Alt previews a trailing point that disappears if Alt is released without clicking, while an Alt-click commits the point and resumes history recording so undo removes the addition as one step.
Releasing a drag of the first or last point while the path visually forms a loop now snaps that endpoint onto the opposite endpoint, closing the shape into a loop.

Resize-handle detection was refactored from a coordinate object to separate pointer coordinates (flagged as a contract risk), so resizing, rotating, and cursor feedback on selected elements must still respond exactly at the pointer.

Selecting exactly one line, arrow, or freehand stroke now shows a guidance hint where the hint area was previously empty, and inside point-editing mode the hint switches between a point-selected and a no-point-selected message.
Hint text is now converted to platform shortcut names, so hints display Cmd on Mac and Ctrl on other systems, with Option for Alt and Delete for Del on Mac.

Shortcut name conversion now matches whole words only, so a Mac label containing the full word Delete now displays exactly Delete instead of being garbled with doubled letters, affecting the shortcuts dialog and button tooltips such as the zoom controls.

Undo history now includes the point-editing state: entering or leaving point-editing mode creates an undo step, moving between points of the same line creates none, and undo and redo restore which line was being edited; confirm this new granularity is intended.

Line, arrow, and freehand-drawn shapes now get their bounding box from a new helper that runs the shape's points through the hand-drawn curve generator and takes the curve's minimum and maximum coordinates; it is used every time a point on a line or arrow is moved, so point dragging recomputes the element's position from curve bounds, and a miscalculation would make the shape visibly jump or drift while dragging.

The global scene was restructured: it now keeps the full element list, a filtered non-deleted list, and an ID-to-element map, and its constructor no longer accepts an initial element list (the app-level scene is created empty and populated wholesale when the scene's elements are replaced); new lookups return an element by ID, or null when that element is deleted.

Line and arrow point editing now resolves elements through these scene lookups across point dragging, pointer move and up handling, finalizing a multi-point drawing, and the delete action, so edits on an element that has been deleted now return null instead of the element; failures would appear as stuck editing, missing updates, or console errors while working with lines and arrows.
Two remaining changes are type-only (points typed as read-only and a type import) with no runtime behavior, so no QA coverage is needed for them.

While editing a line or arrow point by point, Delete now removes only the active point and reselects the previous point (staying on the first point when the first is deleted); previously Delete ran the normal element-deletion path and could not remove points at all.
When the edited line has fewer than two points left, Delete now removes the whole line and exits point-editing mode, and that removal is not recorded as its own history step.

Escape now exits point-editing mode, where it was previously ignored; on exit, a line left with fewer than two points or collapsed to an invisibly small size is deleted from the canvas, and a normal exit is recorded in history.
Escape now also triggers this finalize while a point drag is in progress during line editing, where it was previously ignored.

Deleting a member while editing a group still selects the first remaining group member (unchanged logic, newly extracted), and the code behind undo and redo was refactored to compute the same element list with no intended behavior change.

Verify in a live collaboration session that a point dragged by one participant appears on the other participant's canvas.

Verify that double-clicking with a rectangle selected or with nothing selected still opens the text editor as before.
Verify that pressing Enter with exactly one line or arrow selected enters the same point-editing mode.

Verify that dragging a point handle moves only that point, reshapes the arrow, and that undo restores the previous shape.
Verify that clicking on the canvas while editing grabs or adds points on the arrow rather than starting a new selection, drawing, or resizing action.
Verify that the point under the pointer fills a light red instead of white as you move across the handles, and that the element's normal selection outline stays hidden while editing.
Verify that deleting the selected line while it is being point-edited ends editing cleanly: no leftover point handles, no errors, and the app stays responsive.
Verify that reloading the page while a line is in point-editing mode restores the drawing with editing mode off and normal selection working.
Verify that saving the drawing to a file and reopening it while point-editing does not resume editing mode or misbehave.
Verify that exporting to PNG and copying the image to the clipboard while point-editing produces an output showing only the drawing, without the red point-editing handles.

Test dragging a point of the rotated arrow in one fast motion across the canvas so the pointer leaves the handle area: the same point must stay glued under the cursor for the entire drag, stop exactly where released, and a follow-up drag must pick up a fresh point.
Verify that while dragging on the rotated element, the moved point stays under the cursor and all point handles render exactly on the line's vertices.
Confirm dragging the last point until the path visually closes and releasing snaps it onto the first point (loop closed), while releasing it farther away leaves the gap with no snap.
Check that after a point drag the shape keeps its new geometry and a single undo returns it to the pre-drag state.
Verify the line does not shift or jump when entering edit mode, after exiting edit mode, and after saving and reopening a drawing that contains lines and arrows.

Ensure holding Alt and moving the pointer shows a trailing preview point that follows the cursor, that releasing Alt without clicking removes it, and that an Alt-click commits it so one undo removes the committed addition.

Check that clicking directly on a point lying outside the line's selection box keeps the element in edit mode with that point highlighted instead of deselecting it, and that where two point handles overlap the rightmost one is picked.
Verify that hovering each corner, side, and rotation handle of a selected element shows the correct resize or rotate cursor exactly at the handle position.
Confirm that dragging a corner handle resizes and the rotation handle rotates both a single element and a multi-selection, with the change starting from where the pointer grabbed.
Verify that an exported PNG/SVG and a clipboard image copy show the lines and arrows with correct shape and position, matching what the canvas displays.

Verify that moving between points in point-editing mode without changing anything adds no undo steps: select several different points, then press undo once and confirm it reverts the last real change (for example the last point added) rather than just a point selection.

Test that entering point-editing mode now counts as an undo step: enter the mode, immediately press undo, and confirm the previous state (leaving point-editing mode) is restored rather than an earlier drawing change being reverted, and confirm this is the intended behavior.

Ensure point edits made inside the mode survive undo and redo: move or add points, undo until before the edits and confirm the line shows exactly the previous points, then redo and confirm the edits return.
Verify that selecting exactly one line or arrow with the selection tool shows a point-editing hint; before this change the hint area stayed empty in this situation.
Check that entering point-editing mode on a line, activating a point, and then deactivating it switches the hint between the point-selected and no-point-selected messages.

report.summary: The release adds a toggleable grid to the drawing editor while reworking the core drag, resize, and rotate interactions, including better text resizing.
keyChanges: The editor now supports a toggleable canvas grid that is off by default and draws evenly spaced lines 20 pixels apart at 100% zoom, staying anchored to the drawing while panning and zooming.
The grid setting is now stored when a scene is saved to a file, so reopening a saved scene restores the grid, while scenes saved before this change contain no grid setting and load with the grid off.
PNG exports and clipboard image copies now render the grid when it is enabled, matching what the canvas shows.
Clearing the canvas resets the grid to off because the grid is part of the default editor state.

Moving selected elements and sizing newly drawn shapes were extracted into a new module that the main canvas pointer-move handler now calls, so everyday selection dragging and drawing of new shapes run through new code paths intended to behave exactly as before.

The resize and rotation entry point no longer reads the pointer event itself; the canvas handler now passes three precomputed modifier flags (rotate with discrete angle, resize with sides same length, resize from center), and the rotation and line/arrow endpoint resize functions renamed their angle-lock parameter without logic changes, so Shift-key behaviors must be re-verified.

Text resizing now makes a third font-size measurement, reducing the scale by 1% before giving up: text whose two earlier measurements missed the target box by 1px or more was previously left unchanged and now resizes with a font about 1% smaller than the exact fit, which also affects group resizes that include text.

Grid mode is new: it can be turned on and off from an item added to the end of the right-click menu on empty canvas, and with Ctrl (Cmd on Mac) plus the key that reports key code 222 (the single-quote position on a US layout); that item is intentionally absent from the menu shown when right-clicking on an element.

With the grid on, newly drawn shapes and arrow/line endpoints start on the nearest grid intersection and grow in grid steps, while the freehand draw tool is deliberately exempt from snapping; with the grid off, element creation behaves as before.

With the grid on, dragging snaps to the grid using a grab-point offset so selections land grid-aligned, multi-selection drags go through a shared move routine and stay rigid, and Alt-dragged duplicates land on the grid; with the grid off, dragging should match the previous behavior exactly.
With the grid on, resizing snaps in grid steps while Shift (keep proportions), Alt (resize from center), and Shift's discrete-angle rotation snapping still apply.
With the grid on, arrow keys nudge the selection one grid cell per press and Shift+arrow nudges by the plain-arrow step used before this change; with the grid off, arrow nudging is unchanged.
qaChecks: Verify that with the grid off the canvas shows no grid lines, then turning the grid on draws evenly spaced lines 20 pixels apart at 100% zoom, and turning it off again removes them completely.
Verify that after enabling the grid, panning and zooming keep the lines anchored to the drawing so they re-align cleanly instead of drifting or leaving gaps at the canvas edges.
Verify the shortcuts dialog still opens and shows its complete shortcut list, and that any grid shortcut it lists actually toggles the grid.
Verify a scene saved with the grid on reopens with the grid still on and scenes saved with the grid off reopen with the grid off.
Verify a scene file saved before this change, which carries no grid setting, still opens without errors and loads with the grid off.
Verify a PNG export of a drawing with the grid enabled includes the same grid lines as the canvas, and the same export with the grid off contains no grid.
Verify copying the drawing to the clipboard as an image respects the grid setting the same way as the PNG export.
Verify clearing the canvas resets the grid to off so no grid lines remain on the emptied canvas.

Verify resizing the text element with a corner handle to a box much smaller than the text's natural proportions (for example dragging a long word's corner well past its measured size) applies the resize and updates the font size so the text scales cleanly instead of stretching, ending possibly about 1% smaller than the exact target rather than the text staying unchanged.

Confirm selecting the text element together with a shape and resizing the group by a corner handle completes the group resize and scales the text's font size along with the shape, instead of the resize being blocked by the text.
Verify holding Shift while dragging the rotation handle snaps rotation to fixed steps, and rotating without Shift follows the pointer freely.

Verify holding Shift while dragging an endpoint of a two-point line or arrow snaps the endpoint to discrete angles both when dragging the far end and when dragging from the origin side, and without Shift the endpoint follows the pointer freely.

Verify resizing a shape with the sides-same-length modifier held produces equal sides (square or circle), and resizing with the center-point modifier grows the shape symmetrically from its center, while without modifiers the opposite corner stays anchored.

Verify selecting a single element and then several elements and dragging each selection moves the selection smoothly with the pointer, keeping the relative positions of multiple selected elements unchanged.
Verify drawing a rectangle, ellipse, and diamond by dragging creates each shape at the dragged size and position.

Verify drawing with the sides-same-length modifier held constrains the shape to equal sides (square, circle, or diamond), and drawing with the center-point modifier makes the shape grow outward from the center point.
Verify right-clicking an empty canvas spot opens the context menu normally, ending with a new grid-mode toggle item, and choosing it turns grid mode on.
Check that right-clicking on top of an existing shape shows the element context menu without the grid-mode toggle item.
Test pressing Ctrl (Cmd on Mac) together with the key that reports key code 222 (single-quote position on a US layout) toggles grid mode on, and pressing it again turns it off.
Verify with the grid on, starting a rectangle drag from a spot between grid lines makes the shape start on the nearest grid intersection and size in grid steps as you drag.
Check with the grid on that a dragged-out arrow or line has its endpoints landing on grid intersections while the freehand draw tool still traces the cursor smoothly without snapping.
Ensure with the grid off, every creation tool places and sizes elements exactly as before this change (free positioning, no snapping).
Verify with the grid on, dragging a single shape from a spot between grid lines moves it in one-grid-cell steps so it ends grid-aligned when released.
Check with the grid on, multi-selecting several shapes and dragging still moves them as one rigid group with no relative shifting, and the whole group settles grid-aligned.
Test with the grid on, holding Alt while dragging creates a duplicate that is also grid-aligned; and with the grid off, normal dragging and Alt-duplication behave exactly as before this change.
Verify with the grid on, dragging a corner or edge handle resizes in grid steps so the shape's edges land on grid lines, while Shift still locks proportions and Alt still resizes from the center.
Confirm with the grid on, rotating a shape with Shift held still snaps to discrete angle steps.
Ensure with the grid off, resizing and rotating behave exactly as before this change.

Verify with the grid on, pressing each arrow key moves the selection one grid cell per press and lands it on grid lines, and Shift+arrow moves it by the plain-arrow step used before this change rather than the old Shift+arrow step.
Ensure with the grid off, arrow keys and Shift+arrow nudge the selection exactly as they did before this change.
uncertainty: Scenes shared through the link-sharing flow are saved with a freshly built default state, so the grid setting may not carry over to whoever opens the shared link; confirm whether the grid should persist for shared scenes.

The modifier-key checks moved from the resize code to the canvas handler: the previous code read the pointer event's Shift key directly for rotation and line/arrow endpoint resizing, while the new code relies on the handler computing the same flags; if that computation differs from the previous direct reads, Shift-rotation snapping and Shift-locked endpoint resizing could silently change, and the supplied evidence does not show how the handler computes the flags.

The new menu item's label is looked up in the app's translations, and that lookup fails loudly when a key is missing; the language files were not part of the supplied evidence, so if the grid-mode label was not added (especially for non-English languages), right-clicking empty canvas could fail to open the menu — the first test area's menu check covers this.
